claims.text: Introducing a thin, inert oxide shell can overcome structural or chemical instability of crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles containing five or more metals during catalytic operation at 773–1173 K.
The inert oxide shell acts as a barrier to diffusion of reactive species.
The inert oxide shell reduces nanoparticle exposure to the reactive environment.
Restricting diffusion and environmental exposure preserves the structural stability of the nanoparticles.
Restricting diffusion and environmental exposure preserves the chemical stability of the nanoparticles.
Oxide-coated nanoparticles will be more stable than otherwise identical nanoparticles without the oxide shell.
Oxide-coated nanoparticles will maintain catalytic activity for longer than otherwise identical uncoated nanoparticles.
The proposed stabilization applies across 773–1173 K for exposure periods ranging from several hours to days.
The proposed compositional domain is near-equiatomic solid solutions containing five or more metals.
Stabilization effectiveness may depend on oxide-shell thickness.
Stabilization effectiveness may depend on oxide-shell composition.
Stabilization effectiveness may depend on oxide-shell uniformity.
Stabilization effectiveness may depend on the reactive environment and operating conditions.
